walkthroughs.body_html:
Electricity & Magnetism — a core area of GCSE Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Electricity & Magnetism brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Electricity & Magnetism.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A 12 V supply drives 4 A through a resistor. What is the resistance?
options: 3 Ω
8 Ω

mcqs.q: In a series circuit with two identical bulbs:
options: each bulb gets full supply voltage
current is shared between them
voltage is shared equally
one bulb stays off

mcqs.q: What happens to the current as it goes around a series circuit?
options: Current splits in half at the battery so each direction gets some.
Adding a parallel resistor doubles the voltage available.
It stays the same at every point — current is conserved.
Current gets used up by each component as it flows around the circuit.

mcqs.q: What does voltage (potential difference) across a component represent?
options: Voltage is the 'amount of electricity' flowing through the wire.
Voltage measures how many electrons are stored in a battery.
Current splits in half at the battery so each direction gets some.
The energy transferred per unit charge passing through that component.

mcqs.q: What happens to the total resistance when you add another resistor in parallel?
options: Total resistance decreases — there are more paths for current to flow.
Adding a parallel resistor doubles the voltage available.
Adding any resistor always increases the total resistance.
Current splits in half at the battery so each direction gets some.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Potential difference”?
options: Components in one loop: current is the same everywhere, voltages add to the supply voltage.
The rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t. Measured in amperes (A).
For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to voltage: V = IR.
Energy transferred per unit charge: V = E/Q. Measured in volts (V).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Ohm's law”?
options: Energy transferred per unit charge: V = E/Q. Measured in volts (V).
For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to voltage: V = IR.
The rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t. Measured in amperes (A).
Opposition to current flow: R = V/I. Measured in ohms (Ω).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Resistance”?
options: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to voltage: V = IR.
Opposition to current flow: R = V/I. Measured in ohms (Ω).
Components in one loop: current is the same everywhere, voltages add to the supply voltage.
Energy transferred per unit charge: V = E/Q. Measured in volts (V).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Parallel circuit”?
options: Components in one loop: current is the same everywhere, voltages add to the supply voltage.
Components on separate branches: voltage across each branch is the same, branch currents add to total.
The rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t. Measured in amperes (A).
Opposition to current flow: R = V/I. Measured in ohms (Ω).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Series circuit”?
options: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to voltage: V = IR.
Energy transferred per unit charge: V = E/Q. Measured in volts (V).
Components on separate branches: voltage across each branch is the same, branch currents add to total.
Components in one loop: current is the same everywhere, voltages add to the supply voltage.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Current”?
options: Components on separate branches: voltage across each branch is the same, branch currents add to total.
Components in one loop: current is the same everywhere, voltages add to the supply voltage.
For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to voltage: V = IR.
The rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t. Measured in amperes (A).
